name: cpp-btree (Kronuz)
workload: Google's original 2010 btree_bench: random insert/lookup/fulllookup/delete/queueaddrem/mixedaddrem/fifo/forward-iteration of int32, int64, and string keys/values into btree::set/map (node size 256) vs the STL red-black-tree set/map
claimed_speedup: STL vs B-Tree nanoseconds per op, e.g. BM_set_int32_lookup 1160ns vs 414ns (+64.31%), BM_map_int32_insert 1551ns vs 636ns (+58.99%), BM_set_int32_fwditer 158ns vs 26ns (+83.54%); string keys much smaller gap, e.g. BM_set_string_lookup 1709ns vs 1600ns (+6.38%), and string fifo is actually slower for the btree (-61.01%)
hardware: "pmattis-warp.nyc (4 X 2200 MHz CPUs)" per the embedded 2010 comment; vague/old machine label, not a specific CPU model
tradeoffs: modifying the container invalidates ALL outstanding iterators (not just erased ones, unlike std::map/std::set); btree::set<int32_t> uses ~1 byte/element overhead vs ~16-20 bytes for a red-black-tree set; values are moved within/between nodes on rebalance, so it can lose to std::map when value_type is expensive to move
caveats: the benchmark numbers are a 2010-era comment carried over verbatim from Google's original (now-defunct Google Code) cpp-btree project; this repo does not include the btree_bench benchmark harness itself, so the numbers cannot be reproduced from what's here; hardware is only vaguely identified and compiler/flags are unstated, so this is capped at C despite the original project's rigor; string-key gains are much smaller than integer-key gains and one op (fifo on strings) is actually a regression
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "B-tree container faster than std::map std::set benchmark C++" -> github.com/Kronuz/cpp-btree

name: frozenca/BTree
workload: insert/lookup/erase of 1,000,000 random std::int64_t keys, and separately 1,000,000 std::string keys (length 1-50), into a balanced-tree set, 200 repeats per measurement
claimed_speedup: int64 keys: insert 175.5ms vs std::set 907.1ms, lookup 197.8ms vs 961.9ms, erase 211.3ms vs 990.0ms (roughly 4.7-5.2x); std::string keys: insert 1519.6ms vs 1662.9ms, lookup 1188.3ms vs 1666.2ms, erase 1570.4ms vs 1639.8ms (roughly 1.05-1.4x)
tradeoffs: any insert/erase invalidates iterators (nodes hold multiple keys, unlike std::set's per-node stability); requires C++20; default fanout 64, tunable; optional AVX-512 SIMD path for signed integer/float keys; also offers a disk-backed/memory-mapped variant not present in std::set
caveats: hardware/CPU model is never stated ("in my machine"), so despite a stated compiler+flags and 200x-repeated methodology with stdev/95th percentile reported, this falls short of Tier A and is capped at C; the int64 speedup (~5x) is much larger than the string-key speedup (~1.1-1.4x), so the headline number is workload-dependent
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "B-tree" language:C++ --sort stars

name: libart (Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: red-black tree (the ART paper's own in-memory red-black-tree implementation, algorithmically what std::map/std::set are built on, but not literally libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::map)
workload: single-threaded lookups of existing random 32-bit-integer keys in an index of 65K, 16M, and 256M keys, both dense and sparse key distributions (also a 12-thread/8-way-software-pipelined variant at 16M keys), from the ART paper's micro-benchmarks
claimed_speedup: ART reaches roughly 7-10x the lookup throughput of the paper's red-black tree across the tested sizes (e.g. ~110M lookups/sec for ART vs roughly 10-15M for RB at 65K dense keys) (derived from page data: read off the Fig. 10 bar chart, values approximate, not exact printed numbers); multi-threaded ART is ~1.2-1.7x faster than a chained hash table depending on key density
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.6 (optimization flags not stated in the text)
hardware: Intel Core i7 3930K, 6 cores/12 threads, 3.2GHz (3.8GHz turbo), 12MB shared L3 cache, 32GB quad-channel DDR3-1600 RAM, Linux 3.2 x86-64
stars_or_usage: 836 stars; ART is used in the HyPer main-memory database and has influenced indexing in several modern OLTP/OLAP engines
tradeoffs: keys are limited to fixed-width binary-comparable encodings (signed integers, floats, and strings all need a transform to sort correctly bitwise); path compression and lazy expansion are required to bound worst-case space to ~52 bytes/key; libart (this repo) is an independent open-source C99 implementation of the paper's algorithm, not the authors' original benchmark artifact
caveats: the paper benchmarks ART against ITS OWN red-black-tree implementation (one of "two textbook data structures"), not against libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::map, so treat this as evidence for the ART algorithm versus red-black trees generally rather than a direct std::map micro-benchmark; numbers were read off a bar chart rather than a printed table, so are approximate; this GitHub repo (libart) is a separate, unaffiliated C implementation of the published algorithm and was not itself benchmarked in the paper
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "B-tree" language:C++ (surfaced adjacent radix-tree/learned-index results) + WebFetch of the ART paper PDF (db.in.tum.de/~leis/papers/ART.pdf)

name: RadixMap (radix-map)
workload: Catch2 benchmark harness (Release build), inserting and contains()-looking-up 20,000 std::string keys and, separately, 20,000 double keys
claimed_speedup: 3.2x faster insert / 5.4x faster contains() for string keys; 2.2x faster insert / 2.3x faster contains() for double keys (RadixMap ~111-118ms / ~70-73ms / ~101-104ms / ~46-47ms vs std::map ~366-369ms / ~379-407ms / ~215-234ms / ~100-109ms for the same 20,000-key runs)
tradeoffs: keys limited to std::string or integral/floating-point types with a RadixMapKeyTraits specialization; erase() is a tombstone and does not reclaim compression, so heavy churn grows memory beyond the live entry count; iteration is forward-only (no reverse iterators); +0.0 and -0.0 double keys are treated as distinct, unlike std::map's default std::less
caveats: very new, unstarred, single-author project with no independent scrutiny yet; the README explicitly benchmarks a Release/-O3 build but names neither a compiler version nor a CPU model, so it's capped at C, not A/B; only one key count (20,000) was tested
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "std::map" "faster" language:C++ --sort stars

name: Flat-Map-RB-Tree (dro::FlatMap)
workload: mean random-insertion and mean random-find time for int32 keys, container sizes swept from 100 to 10,000,000 elements; std::map, boost::flat_map, and folly::heap_vector_map plotted alongside dro::FlatMap
claimed_speedup: at 10,000,000 elements: insert ~615ns vs std::map's ~830ns (~1.35x), find ~550ns vs std::map's ~770ns (~1.4x); at 1,000,000 elements: find ~230ns vs std::map's ~440ns (~1.9x) (derived from page data: read off the README's line charts, values approximate, not printed as text/table); dramatically faster than boost::flat_map, whose insert/find times explode past a few thousand elements
hardware: Intel Core i5-9300H CPU @ 2.40GHz (4 cores), isolcpus enabled on cores 2 and 3, Linux kernel 6.10.11-200.fc40.x86_64
tradeoffs: any modifying operation invalidates ALL iterators (std::map only invalidates iterators to erased elements); erased slots are not deallocated until shrink_to_fit() or destruction; key and value types must be default-constructible; author labels the project "Beta Testing" with ~50% test coverage
caveats: the benchmark results are published only as PNG line charts in the README (not as a text/CSV table), so the figures above are approximate readings off the chart, explicitly marked as derived; benchmark code lives in the repo's benchmarks/ directory and hardware+compiler+flags are all stated, which is why this clears Tier A, but only one hardware/compiler configuration was tested and the project itself is pre-1.0/beta
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "red-black tree" "faster" language:C++ --sort stars
